Posted March 11, 2003
Analysis by Richard Cowan

One of the questions in the debate over the Iraq war has been whether or not it meets the criteria for a Just War. It should be understood that this is no mere figure of speech. The concept of a Just War is a part of the catechism of the Roman Catholic Church, and even for non-Catholics, it goes so far back into Christian history that it has a relevance to Western Culture as a whole.

In any case, it is a very useful point of reference for anyone thinking about the subject in an orderly way.

Next, we should recognize that the Drug War really is a war, although former Drug Czar Barry McCaffrey sometimes tried to claim that it is not. In fact, it is very useful to see how real this war actually is.

First, it involves the use of the military, both in other countries and domestically.

G. H. W. Bush invaded Panama with a substantial military force and overthrew the government of a former ally. (Sound familiar?) Currently, the DEAland military is involved in the very real Drug War in Colombia, and other paramilitary branches are involved in Peru and Bolivia. Poor peasants are often caught in the crossfire, as is the case in all wars. (Ironically, the legitimate military activity in Afghanistan has increased the production of opium and hashish.)
See
DEAland Collaborates With Colombia Cartels To Bring Cocaine And Violence To The Caribbean. Island Growers Caught In The Middle.

In DEAland, the military has long been involved in domestic cannabis eradication programs in many states, most notably in California, Hawaii and Kentucky. The military has also been used on the Mexican border long before 9/11, with deadly results. In fact, the most militarized part of the domestic Drug War is aimed at cannabis.

Beyond that, domestic law enforcement has adopted paramilitary techniques to attack homes where they suspect any sort of drug-related activity. Sometimes this involves nothing more than simple possession of cannabis. The fact that American citizens are the targets of the military violence does not mean that it is not really a war. On the contrary, it makes the matter all the more morally urgent.

In short, the Drug War is a real war and hence it is appropriate to ask if it meets the traditional criteria that justify a war. Moreover, it is always appropriate to ask whether the circumstances justify the degree of violence used in any government program. Drug prohibition is no exception.
See
Calling All Quacks: The Therapeutic Police State and the Politicization of Medicine. Doctors Cannot Study The Violence of Cannabis Prohibition. Because They Are The Disease, Not The Cure.
and
New Zealanders Analysis of the Consequences of the Violence of Marijuana Prohibition. Bravo!

Indeed, it is outrageous that this question is being raised more about a prospective attack on a foreign dictatorship than about regular attacks on peaceful citizens of the democracies.

The catechism of the Catholic Church says, " The damage inflicted by the aggressor ... must be lasting, grave, and certain

In this case, the aggressor is drugs and/or the users thereof especially including cannabis, which accounts for half or more of all drug arrests in many countries. The reference to damage that is certain would eliminate such justifications as the Gateway theory which is intended to prevent a small number of cannabis users from possibly going on to hard drugs.
See
The Gateway Theory Won't Die Because It Tells Prohibitionists Something They Want to Believe, But The Truth Tells Them Something They Refuse to Hear.

Moreover, all other means of putting an end to it must have been shown to be impractical or ineffective This criterion means that the Dutch experience must be either misrepresented or ignored.
See
Leading Dutch Anti-Prohibitionists Say, The Quality Of The Drugs-Debate Is Abominable.
and links

It clearly puts the burden of proof on those who advocate the use of force.

In addition, there must be serious prospects of success At this point, it is impossible to argue that there is any prospect of success. Marginal gains are hardly a success.

It goes on to say, the use of arms must not produce evils and disorders graver than the evil to be eliminated " This would mean that for both individuals and for society as a whole, cannabis use would have to be more damaging than the violence of cannabis prohibition. Are individuals harmed more by cannabis or by being arrested? Is society damaged more by cannabis than by 750,000 arrests in DEAland alone, and by the violence inherent in the workings of the criminal justice system?
See
The Theory and Practice of Chaos Analysis By Richard Cowan

The Catechism also teaches that the moral law remains in force, even during armed conflict; non-combatants, wounded soldiers, and prisoners must be treated humanely Now consider this in the context of the wretched conditions in so many prisons.
See
The UK Criminal Justice System Is In Chaos. Prisons Full. More Reasons Cannabis Prohibition Must End.
and
Libertarian Party Press Release Gives Data On Prison Population As It Passes 2 Million.

Also, only combatants may be targeted for violence; the indiscriminate destruction of whole cities or territories is never justified.

Consider that point in the context of the attacks on Andean or Afghan peasants, or the behavior of drug squads in inner cities.

St. Thomas Aquinas and other theologians developed a set of conditions for a just war. However, it was Francisco de Vitoria who added the further condition that the war must be waged using " proper means " (debito modo). How a war is waged is intrinsic to its being just. Can the Drug War meet this test?

Here are some other excerpts from the Catechism on war. I do not think that these teachings can be reconciled with the reality of the Drug War.

2302 By recalling the commandment, " You shall not kill, " (94) our Lord asked for peace of heart and denounced murderous anger and hatred as immoral.

2303 Deliberate hatred is contrary to charity. Hatred of the neighbor is a sin when one deliberately wishes him evil. Hatred of the neighbor is a grave sin when one deliberately desires him grave harm. " But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. " (97).

2304 Respect for and development of human life require peace. Peace is not merely the absence of war, and it is not limited to maintaining a balance of powers between adversaries. Peace cannot be attained on earth without safeguarding the goods of persons, free communication among men, respect for the dignity of persons and peoples, and the assiduous practice of fraternity. Peace is " the tranquility of order. " (98) Peace is the work of justice and the effect of charity.(99)

Jesus has declared: " Blessed are the peacemakers. " (103)

2306 Those who renounce violence and bloodshed and, in order to safeguard human rights, make use of those means of defense available to the weakest, bear witness to evangelical charity, provided they do so without harming the rights and obligations of other men and societies. They bear legitimate witness to the gravity of the physical and moral risks of recourse to violence, with all the destruction and death.(104)

Avoid War

2308 All citizens and all governments are obliged to work for the avoidance of war.

2317 Injustice, excessive economic or social inequalities, envy, distrust, and pride raging among men and nations constantly threaten peace and cause wars.

If there is a punch line to all of this, it would be that the Vatican actually supports the Drug War, specifically including cannabis prohibition. However, this position is not ex cathedra, and hence is not subject to the Doctrine of Papal Infallibility. Good Catholics can and do disagree.

In fact, as the March 24, 1997 edition of National Review magazine noted, " CORRECTION: In " For the Record " (Feb. 24) NR reported that Pope John Paul II wanted the Italian government to ban tobacco as a hard drug. In fact he was talking about marijuana.So the Pope is right about tobacco, though wrong about pot. "

As I like to say, Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be shot at by both sides.
